cues.text: There is a volleyball team at Riverside High School.
The team has a big game in two weeks.
Use be going to for a plan you made before you speak.
The form is am, is or are, then going to, then the base form.
The base form is the dictionary form of a verb: play, practice, serve.
- I am going to play.
Short form: I'm going to play.
- She is going to play.
Short form: She's going to play.
- We are going to play.
Short form: We're going to play.
- Not: Leo is not going to play.
- To ask: Are you going to play?
Yes, I am.
/ No, I'm not.
Coach Carter has eleven players.
But a volleyball team has only six players on the court at one time.
So she is going to choose six players for the first game.
The team is also going to practice rotation.
In volleyball, players rotate.
They move one place on the court.
They go the same way as the hands of a clock.
They do this when their team wins the serve from the other team.
For example, the other team serves, and our team wins the point.
Now it is our turn to serve, so our players rotate.
Why?
After each rotation, a different player serves.
Look at these examples.
We are going to practice every day after school.
Coach Carter is going to choose six players for the first game.
Mia is going to practice her serve on Saturday morning.
Leo is not going to play this week.
He hurt his hand.
In a game, there is often no time to plan.
Then we use will.
Will + the base form talks about the future.
Will is the same for every person: I will, she will, they will.
The short forms are I'll, she'll and they'll.
The not form is will not, or won't.
We use will in three ways.
- For a choice you make right now, at the moment you speak.
- For an offer or a promise: I'll help you.
- When you think something will happen: I think we will win.
Be going to and will both talk about the future.
For plans and choices, the difference is when you decide.
Mia decided last week, so she says: I am going to practice on Saturday.
But in a game, the ball flies fast to Leo.
He has no time to plan.
He decides now and shouts: I'll get it!
For what you think will happen, both are OK.
I think we will win.
I think we are going to win.
Quick choices are very important in volleyball.
Why?
A rally starts with the serve.
It ends when the ball is out of play.
This happens when the ball hits the floor, or when a player breaks a rule.
Then the referee blows a whistle.
This shows that the rally has ended.
The team that wins the rally gets one point.
This is true even if the other team served.
So every ball is important.
A volleyball game has up to five sets.
A set is one part of the game, with its own points.
The team that wins three sets wins the game.
Look at these examples.
The ball is coming to me.
I'll get it!
Your bag looks heavy.
I'll carry it for you.
I will serve well tomorrow.
I promise.
I think we will win this set.
Don't worry, Coach.
We won't give up.
Before the big game, Coach Carter explains the game rules.
Have to + the base form says that something is necessary.
The reason often comes from outside you: a rule, a teacher or a coach.
- I, you, we, they: have to.
- He, she, it: has to.
- The past, for every person: had to.
- To ask: Do we have to practice?
Does she have to serve?
- Not: don't have to, doesn't have to.
It is not necessary.
You can do it, but you don't need to.
Before each serve, the referee blows a whistle.
Then the player who serves has to hit the ball within 8 seconds.
Why?
This way, the game does not stop for long.
Many people think players have to use their hands.
They don't have to!
After the serve, players can hit the ball with any part of the body.
Even a leg is OK.
So when a ball flies low, Leo can save it with his leg.
Look at these examples.
Mia has to serve within 8 seconds.
We have to practice hard before the big game.
Leo had to stay home yesterday.
He was sick.
You don't have to use your hands.
A leg is OK too.
Do we have to practice on Sunday?
No, you don't have to.
Some rules on the court are very strong.
For these rules, we often use must and must not.
Must + the base form says that something is very important or necessary.
Must is the same for every person: I must, he must, they must.
Must not, or mustn't, says that something is not allowed.
Must and have to are close in meaning.
Must often shows the speaker's own strong feeling.
Coach Carter says: You must sleep early tonight!
That is her own idea.
Have to often talks about a rule from outside.
But rule books also use must for very strong rules.
Also, must has no past form.
For the past, use had to: We had to practice on Sunday.
Must not and don't have to are very different.
- You must not catch the ball.
It is not allowed.
- You don't have to jump for every ball.
It is not necessary.
You can choose.
In a rally, players must not catch the ball.
They must hit it.
If a player catches the ball, the other team gets one point.
Players must have a number on their shirt.
The number is on the front and on the back.
This way, the referee knows each player.
Look at these examples.
In a rally, players must not catch the ball.
Players must have a number on their shirt.
Players must not throw the ball.
The server must hit the ball with one hand or arm.
The serve must go over the net.
